title: Witch Hazel (Hamamelis vernalis)
subject: Botanical illustration; Samuel Copeland Palmer; Hamamelis vernalis; Ann Fothergill; Fothergill; Humphrey Marshall; Book
description: Quakers relied on networks to maintain the faith spread across a large area in the 17th and 18th centuries, but they also used these networks to share spiritual messages, news, and botanical specimens. Some Friends involved include names we know, like John Bartram, but we’re going to meet a few more today. Bartram’s most regular English correspondent was Peter Collinson, a London Quaker. They traded plants and seeds regularly and it was through Bartram that Collinson introduced witch hazel to England. Actually, Collinson is credited with having introduced nearly 200 new species of plant into Britain. He started collecting seeds as a young man and an early letter of his describes his botanical adventures as escapes ‘from the hurrys of the town to breathe the air of content and quiet’. His work with plants was recognized and Collinson became a fellow of the Royal Society, of which he remained a fellow for 40 years. He played a key role in providing British collectors with plants from abroad, especially from America. He was responsible for introducing nearly 200 new species of plant into Britain. He also corresponded with and wrote scientific papers with Carl Linnaeus and Benjamin Franklin, as well as Sir Hans Sloane, whose collections were the basis of the British Museum and the British Library. Some plants introduced to Britain by Collinson include Silver Maples, Azaleas, Richweed - Collinsonia canadensis, Smooth Hydrangea , Siberian lily - Lilium pensylvanicum, Wild Sweet William, Rhododendron, Poison Ivy, Elderberry, and Viburnum dentatum.
FHL Connection: Darlington, William, and Peter Collinson. Memorials of John Bartram and Humphry Marshall: With Notices of Their Botanical Contemporaries. Philadelphia: Lindsay & Blakiston, 1849.

title: American Elm (Ulmus Americana)
subject: Historical records; Maps; Trees; American Elm; Botanical illustration; Trees in art; Women artists; Samuel Copeland Palmer
description: There is a legend of a treaty between the Lenni Lenape and William Penn taking place under an elm, the Treaty Tree at Shackamaxon, in 1682. Despite no written record of this happening under an elm, the council by Penn's Elm became iconic. In the 1870s that elm was immortalized in the Frieze of American History in the Rotunda of the US Capitol. Benjamin West painted it in his 1771 painting and Edward Hicks included the ‘Treaty Elm’ in many of his Peaceable Kingdoms in the 19th century. The elm itself fell in a gale in 1810, and there were actual eulogies in newspapers around the country. Souvenir hunters snatched bits of the tree until all that was left was the trunk. Horticulturists took cuttings that grew into second-generation trees. And Penn Treaty Park, which the City of Philadelphia opened in 1894. Historian Jared Farmer wrote in 2019 that the celebrations and veneration of the Treaty Elm references Indigenous tree culture: ‘The early tree-themed peace medals from colonial Pennsylvania owed as much to native symbology as European’. Farmer wrote further: 'The famous Hiawatha wampum belt of the Haudenosaunee — and its oral constitution— which featured the tree under which Mohawks, Oneidas, Onondagas, Cayugas, and Senecas actually and metaphorically buried the hatchetactually and metaphorically buried the hatchet'. While the treaty itself has become associated with the theft of Native lands by colonizers, the symbol of the elm is connected to peace. (Citation: Jared Farmer, 'Taking Liberties with Historic Trees', Journal of American History, Volume 105, Issue 4, March 2019, Pages 815–842)
FHL Connection: Charles Smith Ogden family Papers, RG5-108: a leaf and bark from Penn's Treaty Elm. Plus a lot about the Elm in the Peace Collection

title: Pawpaw (Asimina triloba)
subject: Humphrey Marshall; Book; Pawpaw; Botanical illustration; Samuel Copeland Palmer
description: In 1773, Quaker Humphry Marshall established the second botanical garden in the colonies, after John Bartram, his cousin. He was born in 1722 in Chester County, was educated to the age of 12 in stonemasonry, then worked as a farmer. He became interested in the natural world and started to collect books on the topic and specimens. By 1764, he had accumulated enough land and wealth that he had a greenhouse and an observatory. By 1785, he had published, his Arbustrum Americanum, probably the first published work only about botany. Botanist Francis Pennell mused that ‘One can imagine the man of middle years, after his long hours of farm work, finding time to make nearly all its descriptions from actual living plants in his garden or in the woods of Chester County. Each genus and each species received a short but clear account…’ Called by some the "Father of American Dendrology", Marshall corresponded with Peter Collinson and John Fothergill, both of them in England. He also exchanged letters with Sir Hans Sloane, whose collections formed the origins of the British Museum. Paw Paw is native to eastern North America and Marshall found it during his studies of Pennsylvania plantlife for Arbustrum Americanum. He noted that ‘This grows common in rich bottoms or by river sides, in Pennsylvania… The fruit is often found growing two or three together, which soon falls off, becomes very mellow and turns of a yellow color'. (p. 10) (Citations: Pennell, F.W. (1935). 'Humphry Marshall, Botanist'. Bulletin of Friends' Historical Association 24(2), 77-82 and Marshall, H. (1785). Arbustrum Americanum: the American grove: or, An alphabetical catalogue of forest trees and shrubs, natives of the American United States... Joseph Crukshank)

title: Dwarf Fothergilla (Fothergilla gardenii)
subject: Memoir; Biography; John Fothergill; Fothergill; Portrait; Humphrey Marshall; Book
description: According to our friends at the Morris Arboretum, Carl Linnaeus named Dwarf Fothergilla (Fothergilla gardenii) in honor of Quaker John Fothergill, who imported it from America for his Essex garden. Fothergill was an English Quaker physician and plant dealer in the 18th century. He never visited America but he opened his home to many American visitors in the 1700s. In 1762, Fothergill acquired an estate in Essex, outside of London, where he could delve into his botanical interests through a large garden of rare plants sent to him by John Bartram and Humphry Marshall, Pennsylvania Quaker botanists. Marshall, in fact, sent Fothergill 44 different specimens. Marshall packed and sent at least ten boxes from Chester County to Fothergill’s estate between 1767 and 1775. Fothergill was a very busy man, known for his botanical practices, as a host and correspondent, and his abolitionist stance and friendship with well-known abolitionist Anthony Benezet. Just to add, there are other plants named after Quakers out and about in the world, such as Darlingtonia californica (the pitcher plant, a carnivorous plant, named for William Darlington) and Collinsonia canadensis, or richweed, named for Peter Collinson.

title: White Oak (Quercus alba)
subject: Historical records; Maps; Trees; Botanical illustration; Trees in art; White Oak; Women artists; Samuel Copeland Palmer; Quercus alba
description: William Darlington was a physician and botanist in Chester County. To many historians, he is known for having served as a Democratic-Republican member of the House of Representatives from 1819 to 1823. In the plant sciences, Darlington is known for being Humphry Marshall's biographer and an amateur botanist. He wrote about the plants Marshall placed about his home, as well as about plants in Chester County. For Darlington, studying the natural world was an important human activity. He wrote, ‘It is impossible for any one, endowed with the common attributes of humanity, to avoid being something of a Naturalist’. And like many of us, he felt that ‘There is a calm delight in the contemplation of Plants and Flowers, which is never felt - and can never be appreciated - by those who find their chief gratification in the turmoils and commotions of the animal world’. In his 1837 book, Flora cestrica: an attempt to enumerate and describe the flowering and filicoid plants of Chester County in the state of Pennsylvania, he wrote about White Oak, saying, 'This is one of our finest and most valuable forest trees - often attaining to an enormous size… The bark is astringent and tonic - while the acorns are sweet and nutritious, affording a favorite food for swine'. Darlington referred to oaks, in general, as a noble genus. The pride and ornament of our American forests’. (Citation: Darlington, William. Flora Cestrica: An Attempt to Enumerate and Describe the Flowering and Filicoid Plants of Chester County... Printed for the author by S. Siegfried, and for sale by Kimber and Sharpless, Philadelphia, 1837)

title: Franklinia (Monadelphia Polyandria)
subject: Humphrey Marshall; Book; Franklinia; Botanical illustration; Samuel Copeland Palmer
description: Franklinia is obviously named for a very famous non-Quaker but was called so in honor of John Bartram's good friend, Benjamin Franklin, by William Bartram. The Bartrams, father and son, contributed greatly to the Quaker consideration of nature sustainability. John and William lived in Philadelphia but both traveled and collected plants and seeds, which John used to create his famous garden. They benefited from connections all around the Atlantic world, including with Peter Collinson and his son Michael of London, where as both botanists and merchants, they could arrange for the trade and shipping of plants and seeds to and from the Bartrams. Franklinia is in the tea family. William Bartram first observed it in Georgia in October 1765 and returned several times to that same spot on collecting trips funded by John Fothergill. William brought seeds to Philadelphia in 1777 and spent years studying the tree.
FHL Connection: Bartram manuscript letters, loads of books about the Bartrams

title: Roses (Rosa)
subject: Botanical illustration; Flowers in art; Roses; Women artists; Rose garden; Dean Bond; Historical records; Maps; Dean Bond Rose Garden
description: Elizabeth Powell Bond was the first Dean of Women at Swarthmore College, a position she held from 1890 to 1906. A birthright Quaker and lifelong member of the Society of Friends, she played an important role in the development of coeducation at the College. She was born in New York state in 1841 and attended the State Normal School in Albany, then became an instructor in calisthenics at Vassar. In 1886, Swarthmore College appointed Bond Matron of the College and, four years later, she was named Dean, a position she held for 20 years. During that time, she was a member of Swarthmore Monthly Meeting. Dean Bond was an avid gardener, and when the old tennis courts were removed from this spot, the rose garden was established in her honor.

title: Climbing Aster (Ampelaster carolinianus)
subject: Botanical illustration; Flowers in art; Asters; Women artists;  Botanical illustration; Ann Fothergill; Fothergill; Ampelaster carolinianus
description: Graceanna Lewis is a favorite of Friends Historical Library staff and maybe we can interest you in reading more about her. She was a Quaker Ornithologist, botanist and activist from Chester County. She joined both the Academy of Natural Sciences and the Delaware County Institute of Science, scientific societies that gave Lewis access to scientific networks. She published papers, gave lectures, and exhibited her research. As with other women scientists of this time period, her lack of degree meant that she was considered an “amateur.” Sadly the work of women who practiced science by mingling it with everyday life, art, and literature became less visible as academia defined stricter representations of science. In 1885, Lewis retired to Media, just down the road from the College, which was and is the home of the Delaware County Institute of Science. Lewis is mentioned in this tour as a natural scientist, but others know her better as an abolitionist and activist for women’s suffrage. Letters in the Friends Historical Library document her experience working in the Underground Railroad. Lewis illustrated many plants and flowers, including various types of asters, which we can see here.

title: Red Maple (Acer rubrum)
subject: Botanical illustration; Trees in art;  Women artists; Samuel Copeland Palmer; Acer rubrum
description: Humphry Marshall, discussed earlier in this tour, also wrote about the Red Maple in his book, Arbustrum Americanum. Writing about about the ‘Science of Botany’, Marshall said ‘it is an object highly deserving the attention of Mankind in general… but in a particular manner of the inhabitants of this Commonwealth’. ‘Those who are conversant in trade well know the continual enormous expence we are at in purchasing foreign Teas, Drugs, Dye-Stuffs, &c. The diminution of this, ought to be the care and concern of every friend to his Country’s welfare. And we presume it will appear evident, that the most eligible and obvious means may lead to this delightful science…’  The Red Maple itself 'grows to a pretty large size in rich soil... There is a variety of this with yellowish flowers and seeds, which is, I believe, the most common kind in Pennsylvania'. (p.3) (Citation: Marshall, H. (1785). title: Meal Tree / Viburnum (Viburnum dentatum)
subject: Botanical illustration; Samuel Copeland Palmer; Humphrey Marshall; Book; Viburnum dentatum
description: Priscilla Wakefield was an English Quaker philanthropist and author who wrote books on feminism, economics, and science. From her 1796 book, An introduction to Botany, Wakefield wrote about the Meal Tree, or what we more commonly call viburnum. She wrote that its blossom with 'a small cup superior to the seed-vessel, with five teeth; one bell-shaped petal, with five hollow clefts turned back; its fruit a roundish berry of one cell, concealing a single seed as hard as a bone'. From her 1798 Reflections on the Present Condition of the Female Sex, ‘There are many branches of science, as well as useful occupations, in which women may employ their time and their talents, beneficially to themselves and to the community, without destroying the particular characteristic of the sex… And here the author may be allowed to express her hope, that among the numbers of the female world, who appear to be satisfied with their own inferiority, many require only to be awakened to a true sense of their real consequence…’ She wrote that women could study many subjects, including botany. To place Wakefield in context, both she and Mary Wollstonecraft recommended education to enable women to be financially self-supporting. They also agreed that women and men should be paid equal wages for equal work. They differed in how to achieve equal rights, however, with Wajefield preferring a more moderate approach to Wollstonecraft. (Citation: Wakefield, Priscilla. An Introduction to Botany, in a Series of Familiar Letters. Printed for E. Newberry, [etc.], 1796 and Wakefield, Priscilla. Reflections on the Present Condition of the Female Sex, with Suggestions for Its Improvement. 1798)

title: Scott Arboretum Founding
subject: Historical records; Botanical illustration; Swarthmore College Scott Arboretum; Scott Arboretum Founding; Gardens
description: The Scott Arboretum & Gardens is named for Arthur Hoyt Scott, a member of the Class of 1895 and second president of Scott Paper Company, whose family established a horticultural foundation in his name in 1929. Encompassing more than 300 acres of Swarthmore's campus and exhibiting more than 4,000 kinds of ornamental plants, the Arboretum displays some of the best trees, shrubs, vines, and perennials for use in the region. The arboretum was contructed around the campus architcture and in 1915, Hoyt Scott planted 100 lilacs to beautify the Swarthmore Campus. According the the book, "The Scott Arboretum of Swarthmore College: The first 75 years" by Ben Yagoda, there was resistence from the college administration to the project. The aboretum under its many directors has the mission, initially conceived by Scott, to educate the public and college community.
